title: PathWatch — Network Path Monitoring and Rust Edge Proxy: Hybrid BGP/BFD Failover, CUSUM Path-Change Detection, Envoy/NGINX Benchmark

workstreams.title: Hybrid WireGuard + FRR eBGP/BFD failover between an Azure NVA and an on-prem router
workstreams.summary: Terraform-managed Azure networks in westus and francecentral plus a hybrid link: an FRR network virtual appliance in Azure westus and an on-prem router container on a workstation run two WireGuard tunnels with one eBGP session each, the primary preferred by local-pref. A failover drill drops the primary tunnel's UDP 51820 in both directions (interfaces stay up), times the switch to the backup route in the kernel (250 ms polling) and the longest gap in a 100 ms ping stream between two private workloads. Both tunnels share one NVA, one host and one physical path, so the drill measures failure detection, not high availability. The Terratest run covers network configuration only; the Private DNS / Traffic Manager failover, the remote-state CI workflow and any region failover were not completed.
bullets: Cut median route failover on a hybrid WireGuard + FRR eBGP link (Azure westus NVA to an on-prem router container) from 172.456 s with BGP 60/180 s timers to 8.535 s with 3/9 s and 1.201 s with BFD (300 ms × 3), 5 trials per profile, measured by dropping the primary tunnel's UDP in both directions and timing the kernel route switch; both tunnels share one NVA and one physical path.
Measured the longest gap in a 100 ms ping stream between two private workloads at 172.035 s, 8.251 s and 0.839 s for the same three timer profiles.

Traced a first failover campaign that never switched routes within 230 s to a one-way drop that let the two BGP speakers expire their hold timers at different times and to FRR 8.4.4 keeping graceful-restart helper mode on under `no bgp graceful-restart`; the passing campaign drops both directions and uses `bgp graceful-restart-disable`.

Provisioned regional Azure networks with Terraform modules; Terratest created, checked (subnets, NSG rules including default deny, route tables) and destroyed 14 network resources in each of westus and francecentral (PASS in 134.19 s and 153.27 s), network configuration only, with no VMs or cross-region traffic in that test.

workstreams.title: Go network probes, ClickHouse ingest with outage backfill, and CUSUM path-change detection
workstreams.summary: Go probe agent running DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP/1.1-3 and traceroute measurements with a scheduler and a durable on-disk spool that retries until acknowledged; a Go ingest service (stateless frontend, core with journal) that deduplicates by batch and stores results in ClickHouse; and a CUSUM job that flags latency shifts per path, uses traceroute snapshots to say whether the route changed and at which hop, and since 2026-11-01 latches after an alarm so a lasting shift alarms once. Measured on one shared workstation: one probe, a three-hop Docker lab and simulations.
bullets: Backfilled every result after a 1,200.4 s ingest outage in a single-probe drill on one machine: both burn-rate pages fired (after 30.436 s and 605.464 s) and the probe's durable spool drained 70 results in 11 batches with 0 duplicate (batch key, result index) rows and 0 spool drops.

Chose the CUSUM alarm threshold H = 12 by a rule fixed before a 2,000-trial simulation (K = 0.5, 10,000 windows per trial): P(no false alarm) 0.9875 with a known baseline and 6σ steps caught in 2.76 windows on average; with the 20-window estimated baseline the job uses, P(no false alarm) drops to 0.7455.

Detected a real route change in a three-hop Docker lab in the first 5-minute window (TCP p95 20.633 ms vs a 0.358 ms baseline) and attributed it to the hop at TTL 2 from traceroute snapshots, with no alarm in the 21 windows before.

Made the CUSUM detector latch after an alarm instead of resetting, with the rule and its test written before measuring (sum clamped at H, re-armed after at least 24 baseline windows, 2 hours): in simulation on resampled lab noise a lasting shift alarmed once in 36 windows instead of 4 / 7.0 / 12 / 36 times with reset for 2 / 3 / 6 / 20 ms shifts, and mean false alarms per 10,000 windows with the 20-window baseline fell from 5.862 to 3.075; not yet run in a live recording.
Ran the ingest store against a ClickHouse testcontainer: 8 of 9 full runs passed; one failed after a container restart left ClickHouse not answering HTTP, cause not found.

workstreams.title: Rust L7 edge proxy benchmarked against Envoy and NGINX
workstreams.summary: Rust L7 edge proxy on tokio, hyper and rustls: TLS/SNI, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, connection pooling, power-of-two-choices least-request and Maglev load balancing, active and passive health checks, a retry budget and SIGHUP hot reload. Benchmarked against Envoy and NGINX with fixed-rate load through TLS 1.3 to one backend, each proxy on the same two pinned cores, 4 rates × 5 rounds × 120 s per proxy and protocol, on one workstation that also ran other projects. 30 s diagnostic cells (3 rounds) then compared one vs two tokio workers and a per-core runtime prototype on the remaining HTTP/2 gap to NGINX.
bullets: Cut the edge proxy's HTTP/2 p50 at 10k rps from 10.168 ms to 0.342 ms by setting TCP_NODELAY on accepted downstream sockets, after the first benchmark showed a 10 ms p50 plateau from Nagle's algorithm holding responses until the client's delayed ACK (runs on different days, one machine).

Benchmarked against Envoy 1.39.5 and NGINX 1.30.6 in one run (TLS 1.3, one backend, 4 rates × 5 rounds × 120 s, proxies on the same two pinned cores): p50 at 10k rps HTTP/2 0.318 / 0.861 / 0.108 ms and HTTP/1.1 1.070 / 1.750 / 0.980 ms, lower p50 and p99 than Envoy at every rate, above NGINX on HTTP/2 latency and on CPU per request.

Measured two options for the remaining HTTP/2 gap to NGINX in 30 s diagnostic cells (3 rounds): one tokio worker instead of two cut the 1k p50 from 0.455 to 0.216 ms but raised p99 from 3.166–3.167 to 10.664–10.671 ms, and a per-core prototype (current-thread runtimes with SO_REUSEPORT listeners and their own upstream pools) used 6–13% less CPU per request but was worse at 20k rps (p50 0.866 vs 0.314 ms, p99 31.09 vs 4.14 ms), so the multi-thread runtime stayed the default.
Built power-of-two-choices least-request and Maglev load balancing, active and passive health checks, a retry budget and SIGHUP hot reload on tokio, hyper and rustls.

workstreams.title: Argo Rollouts canary rollback and graceful pod deletion on kind, and BGP leak/hijack detection on Docker networks
workstreams.summary: Helm charts, an Argo CD app-of-apps and an Argo Rollouts canary for the ingest frontend, whose pods carry the Rust edge proxy as a native sidecar, on a single-node kind cluster (Kubernetes 1.36.4, Argo CD 3.5.6, Argo Rollouts 1.10.1, Prometheus 3.14.0) with desired state in a local Git repository. The canary fails if more than 5% of the candidate's queries fail over 1 minute or if it served fewer than 5, so no data is a failure. A synthetic client sends 20 queries/s, each on a new connection, and from 2026-11-01 also 2 Report RPCs/s (the probes' gRPC upload call) on one long-lived connection. Drills: bad-build rollbacks and good-build promotions (10-27, 10-28, 11-01, 11-06) and deletions of the frontend pod holding the Report connection, before and after a drain fix (11-06). Plus a BGP lab on plain Docker networks, not containerlab: nine FRR 10.7.1 routers (three anycast PoPs announcing one /24, two transit ASes, three customer ASes), a GoBGP 4.10.0 collector, RPKI from a Krill 0.16.0 test trust anchor and Routinator 0.15.3, and a detector for route leaks and hijacks. Everything ran on one shared workstation.
bullets: Cut canary rollback of a build returning HTTP 500 from 41.7–43.1 s to 22.1–22.9 s after the commit (3 drills each, single-node kind cluster, Argo Rollouts with a Prometheus error-rate analysis) by going from 2 replicas, a 50% first step and a 40 s initial delay to 4 replicas, 25% and 20 s; clients saw non-200 responses for about 22 s instead of about 41 s (15.81–18.28% of requests in each drill window instead of 44–46%), and a good build was promoted at 75.4 s.

Removed the good-build control's 17/1,560 non-200 responses with a 10 s preStop sleep on the frontend, after finding that pod deletion removed the endpoint and sent SIGTERM at the same moment while kube-proxy and the sidecar still routed queries to it: 3 control drills then had 2/1,600, 0/1,600 and 1/1,620 non-200 (all admission 429s, also seen in steady state), and 5 bad-build drills rolled back in 22.0–23.5 s.

Cut Report RPC failures per frontend pod deletion from 160–161 of 212–214 (an 81 s window) to 0 of 50–54 over 5 deletions each on kind, after container exit codes and conntrack showed the Rust edge-proxy sidecar, running as PID 1 and handling only SIGINT, held the client's long-lived gRPC connection until it was SIGKILLed at the end of the 90 s grace period; the frontend's preStop hook now tells the proxy to drain (HTTP/2 GOAWAY while the pod still serves) and the proxy handles SIGTERM, so the pod is gone after 10.9–11.5 s instead of 91.0–91.7 s.

Detected BGP route leaks 5/5 in 0.167–0.415 s and /25 hijacks 5/5 as RPKI-invalid in 0.178–0.426 s with 0.25 s polling in an anycast lab of nine FRR routers on Docker networks (3 PoPs, 2 transit ASes, 3 customer ASes, RPKI from Krill and Routinator), with 0 alerts in the baseline.
